subject: history

facts.claim: Non-genetic heredity of effects from events like famine is often mediated by epigenetic regulations of gene expression and may be transferred even across several generations.
facts.quote: This heredity is often mediated by epigenetic regulations of gene expression and may be transferred even across several generations.

facts.claim: Methodological shortcomings in studies of the 20th-century Dutch and Chinese famines may have led to the misinterpretation of some findings.
facts.quote: Such methodological shortcomings may have led to the misinterpretation of some findings.
facts.causalWarning: causal wording, but the cited study only shows an association

facts.claim: The effects of famine might be heritable through epigenetics.
facts.quote: research on the Dutch Hunger Winter (1944–1945), which indicated transgenerational transmission of biological effects through epigenetics (i.e., that the effects of famine might be “heritable”).

facts.claim: POMC DNA methylation in children is linked to elevated lipids and insulin, independent of body habitus.
facts.quote: Studies in children propose a link between POMC DNA methylation and elevated lipids and insulin, independent of body habitus.

facts.claim: Stress exposure from events like famine is linked to changes in hormonal production, the HPA axis, cognition, behavior, or a propensity to certain psychiatric or metabolic disorders.
facts.quote: The reviewed studies show a plethora of universal changes which stress exposure initiates on multiple levels of organisation ranging from hormonal production and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis modulation all the way to cognition, behaviour, or propensity to certain psychiatric or metabolic disorders.

facts.claim: POMC DNA methylation is linked to maternal nutrition in early pregnancy and is associated with childhood and adult obesity.
facts.quote: Recent human studies suggest POMC DNA methylation is influenced by maternal nutrition in early pregnancy and associated with childhood and adult obesity.

research.angle: Historical famine and early-life nutritional deprivation are linked to transgenerational epigenetic changes that may influence metabolic health and disease risk in descendants.
research.verdict: The sources provide evidence that famine and early-life nutrition can cause epigenetic changes and metabolic programming that may be passed across generations.
research.caveat: Some existing studies on the Dutch and Chinese famines may contain methodological shortcomings that could lead to the misinterpretation of findings.
